query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys, exposure to cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures induces localized solute redistribution at grain boundaries, leading to a reduction in grain-boundary cohesion and the emergence of brittle behavior, even though the alloy remains nominally single‐phase.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with uniform elemental distribution and high toughness.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to cyclic loading at temperatures typical of service conditions (e.g., a moderately elevated temperature relevant to high-temperature applications) over an extended period.
generation.conditions: Cyclic mechanical loading combined with an elevated temperature environment, under service-relevant atmospheres, to simulate realistic operational stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain boundaries act as mediators where stress-enhanced diffusion leads to local compositional segregation.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical loading accelerates the diffusion of specific alloying elements toward grain boundaries, where their accumulation reduces the interatomic binding energy and cohesion at these boundaries. This localized chemical inhomogeneity disrupts the ductile deformation pathways, facilitating crack initiation and brittle fracture, which contrasts with the behavior expected from conventional alloys where grain-boundary segregation is typically linked to precipitation rather than stress-driven in situ modifications.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline state, the treated samples will exhibit measurable decreases in toughness (e.g., lower fracture toughness or impact energy) and evidence of grain-boundary chemical heterogeneity (as detected by TEM/EDS analysis). This effect is expected to be more pronounced under conditions combining cyclic load and elevated temperature.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated alloy with a homogeneous single-phase microstructure and uniform grain-boundary composition, exhibiting high toughness under standard testing.
generation.boundary: Results are applicable within service conditions that involve cyclic loading and elevated temperatures; deviations in alloy composition or significantly different loading regimes may alter the outcome.
generation.uncertainty: The extent to which stress-induced segregation occurs and its quantitative impact on toughness may vary with alloy composition and the magnitude/duration of the applied loading. The precise kinetics of segregation and its threshold for embrittlement remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. One set serves as a control (maintained at room temperature without cyclic loading), while the experimental sets are subjected to cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures that mimic service conditions for a predefined duration. After treatment, carry out detailed microstructural and mechanical testing.
measurements: Grain-boundary composition using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Fracture toughness (e.g., via Charpy impact tests or standardized fracture mechanics tests)
Stress-strain curves to assess ductility and yield behavior
Quantification of micro-crack density and initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cyclically loaded samples do not show statistically significant grain-boundary compositional changes or a reduction in toughness relative to the control samples, or if the observed brittleness can be explained solely by phenomena known in conventional alloys (e.g., precipitation without stress-induced segregation), then the hypothesis is falsified.
